questions.question: A security assessor wants to scan a Windows Server 2008 R2 machine to identify missing patches, weak security configurations, and blank or weak local account passwords. Which Microsoft tool was designed specifically for this purpose on legacy Windows systems?

options.A: Microsoft Baseline Security Analyzer (MBSA), which scans for missing updates, common misconfigurations, and weak account policies
options.B: Microsoft Security Compliance Toolkit (SCT), which deploys Group Policy Objects to enforce CIS benchmark settings
options.C: Windows Server Update Services (WSUS), which distributes and approves Windows Updates to managed endpoints
options.D: System Center Configuration Manager (SCCM), which provides enterprise-wide software deployment and inventory collection

questions.explanation: Microsoft Baseline Security Analyzer (MBSA) is a free tool designed to assess individual machines or small networks for common security misconfigurations. It checks for missing Windows and application patches (via the Microsoft Update catalogue), blank or weak passwords on local accounts, IIS and SQL Server configuration issues, and unnecessary services. MBSA produces a prioritised report suited to manual security review. Note that MBSA was deprecated by Microsoft and its last version (2.3) does not support Windows 10 or Server 2016 and later — on modern systems, Windows Update, Microsoft Defender, or SCCM-based compliance scanning have replaced it. WSUS is a patch distribution server — it does not scan for vulnerabilities. SCCM/MECM provides enterprise endpoint management including patch deployment but is not a dedicated security assessment scanner. The Security Compliance Toolkit applies and audits Group Policy baselines rather than scanning for missing patches.

questions.question: An organisation is choosing between WSUS and SCCM (now Microsoft Endpoint Configuration Manager) for their patch management strategy. What is the primary capability that SCCM provides that WSUS alone does not?

options.A: SCCM manages patching for a wide range of third-party applications and non-Microsoft software in addition to Windows updates, and provides full software deployment, inventory, and compliance reporting across the enterprise
options.B: WSUS can only distribute patches to Windows 10 endpoints, whereas SCCM supports all Windows versions including Windows Server 2003 and earlier legacy systems
options.C: SCCM uses a push model where clients contact the server on demand, while WSUS uses a pull model that requires an administrator to manually initiate each patch deployment
options.D: WSUS requires each client to have a paid Software Assurance licence, whereas SCCM is included free with all Windows Server editions

questions.explanation: WSUS (Windows Server Update Services) is purpose-built for distributing Microsoft product updates — Windows OS, Office, and selected Microsoft applications. It does not natively patch third-party software such as Adobe Reader, Java, browsers, or other vendors' products. SCCM (now MECM) integrates with the Software Update Point role to extend patch management to third-party applications via catalogues, and also provides software deployment, hardware and software inventory, compliance reporting, OS deployment, and endpoint telemetry. This breadth makes SCCM the enterprise choice when comprehensive patch coverage is required. The licensing and architecture points in the other options are factually incorrect.

questions.question: The ProxyLogon vulnerability chain (CVE-2021-26855) affecting Microsoft Exchange allowed pre-authentication remote code execution. Which Exchange component did ProxyLogon primarily abuse to bypass authentication?

options.A: The Exchange Control Panel (ECP) server-side request forgery via the Client Access Service
options.B: The Autodiscover endpoint by injecting commands into the XML configuration response
options.C: The Outlook Web Access (OWA) login form through a cross-site request forgery token leak
options.D: The SMTP relay service by sending specially crafted email headers to the transport agent

questions.explanation: ProxyLogon abused a server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in the Exchange Client Access Service (CAS). The SSRF (CVE-2021-26855) allowed an unauthenticated attacker to send crafted requests through the CAS frontend that were forwarded internally with SYSTEM-level trust to backend services, including the Exchange Control Panel (ECP). By targeting ECP through this SSRF, the attacker could impersonate any user without credentials. This was then chained with a post-auth arbitrary file write vulnerability (CVE-2021-27065) in the ECP to achieve remote code execution. ProxyLogon was one of the most severe Exchange vulnerabilities ever disclosed, affecting millions of on-premises servers.

questions.question: During a penetration test you discover that Exchange is deployed on-premises and is joined to the Active Directory domain. An attacker on the internal network could potentially coerce Exchange to authenticate outbound and relay those credentials. Which attack technique best describes this?

options.A: NTLM relay via Exchange's EWS or Autodiscover endpoints using tools such as PrivExchange
options.B: Kerberoasting the Exchange service account to recover its plaintext password offline
options.C: AS-REP roasting the Exchange computer account because pre-authentication is disabled
options.D: DCSync abuse of the Exchange Windows Permissions group to dump all domain hashes

questions.explanation: Exchange traditionally held the 'Exchange Windows Permissions' group membership and could write ACLs on the domain object. The PrivExchange technique forces Exchange to authenticate to an attacker-controlled host via its EWS or Autodiscover push-notification feature. The attacker then relays the resulting NTLM authentication to the Domain Controller's LDAP service. Because Exchange's machine account has high AD privileges, this relay can be used to grant any user DCSync rights, effectively compromising the entire domain. Kerberoasting and AS-REP roasting are different credential attacks, and DCSync is a consequence of the relay rather than the initial technique.

questions.question: An attacker places a malicious DLL in a directory that is searched by a Windows application before the legitimate system directory. Which vulnerability class does this technique exploit?

options.A: DLL search-order hijacking, exploiting the application's failure to specify an absolute path
options.B: Unquoted service path exploitation, inserting an executable in a path segment with spaces
options.C: COM object hijacking, replacing a HKCU registry key to redirect object instantiation
options.D: Binary planting via a shared network drive mapped to the application's working directory

questions.explanation: Windows resolves DLL dependencies by searching a defined list of directories in order (the 'DLL search order'). If an application loads a DLL by name only, without a fully qualified path, Windows searches the application directory, the current working directory, system directories, and other locations. An attacker who can write to any directory earlier in that search order can place a malicious DLL with the same name and have it loaded instead of the legitimate one. This is known as DLL search-order hijacking and is commonly used for privilege escalation or persistence. It is distinct from unquoted service paths, COM hijacking, and network share planting, which are separate but related techniques.

questions.question: A Windows service is configured with the binary path: C:\Program Files\My App\service.exe. No quotation marks surround the path. What is the security risk of this configuration?

options.A: Windows may interpret 'C:\Program' as the executable and 'Files\My' as an argument, allowing privilege escalation via a planted binary
options.B: The service will fail to start because Windows requires all service paths to use 8.3 short filenames
options.C: Any user can replace the service.exe binary because spaces in paths disable ACL enforcement
options.D: The Service Control Manager will grant the service SYSTEM privileges automatically if the path contains spaces

questions.explanation: When Windows encounters an unquoted service binary path that contains spaces, it attempts to resolve the executable by progressively appending '.exe' to each space-delimited segment. For a path like 'C:\Program Files\My App\service.exe', Windows first tries to execute 'C:\Program.exe'. If a low-privileged user can write to C:\ (which is sometimes possible), placing a file named 'Program.exe' there will cause it to run as the service's user — often SYSTEM. This unquoted service path vulnerability is a classic Windows privilege escalation technique. Quotation marks around the path completely eliminate this risk.

questions.question: An NFS share on a target server is mounted by an attacker who creates a local user with UID 1001 to match the owner of protected files on the share. Which NFS weakness does this technique abuse?

options.A: NFS relies on client-side UID/GID values for access control, so spoofing the UID grants file access
options.B: NFS transmits file contents in cleartext, so the attacker sniffs the data from the network wire
options.C: The 'no_subtree_check' export option causes the server to skip all permission checks entirely
options.D: NFSv3 uses weak MD5 checksums that can be forged to impersonate any authenticated user

questions.explanation: NFSv3 and earlier versions trust the UID and GID reported by the NFS client's kernel without any independent verification on the server. If an export does not use Kerberos authentication (AUTH_GSS) and root_squash is the only protection, an attacker with root on their own machine can simply create a local account with the same UID as the target file owner and mount the share to gain full access to those files. This is UID spoofing and is a fundamental weakness of host-trust-based NFS. NFSv4 with Kerberos (krb5p) prevents this by binding authentication to principal names rather than numeric IDs.

questions.question: When reviewing an NFS server's /etc/exports file, you see the entry: /data *(rw,no_root_squash). What does the asterisk (*) wildcard indicate in this context?

options.A: Any host on any network is permitted to mount the /data share with read-write and root access
options.B: Only hosts whose hostname matches a wildcard DNS record in the local zone can mount the share
options.C: The share is exported anonymously and all users are mapped to the 'nobody' account regardless
options.D: The asterisk enables NFS over UDP only, restricting TCP-based mounts from remote networks

questions.explanation: In /etc/exports, the client specification field defines which hosts are permitted to mount the share. An asterisk (*) is a wildcard that matches any hostname or IP address, meaning the export is accessible to every host on the internet or local network without restriction. Combined with 'rw' (read-write) and 'no_root_squash' (remote root retains root privileges), this is one of the most dangerous NFS misconfigurations possible. A secure configuration should always restrict the client list to specific IP addresses or CIDR ranges, such as: /data 192.168.1.0/24(rw,root_squash).

questions.question: Which system-wide file, if misconfigured, allows any user from a listed remote host to log in via rlogin or rsh without a password, regardless of individual user .rhosts files?

options.A: /etc/hosts.equiv, which grants trust to entire hosts for all non-root users system-wide
options.B: /etc/passwd, which stores cleartext passwords that rlogin reads to grant passwordless access
options.C: /etc/shadow, which is parsed by rshd to determine which accounts allow remote trust
options.D: /etc/inetd.conf, which maps R-service trust relationships to specific TCP port numbers

questions.explanation: The /etc/hosts.equiv file is a system-wide trust configuration. Each line lists a hostname (and optionally a username), and any user connecting from a listed host is permitted to log in to a matching local account without providing a password. Unlike the per-user ~/.rhosts file, /etc/hosts.equiv affects all non-root users on the system, making a misconfigured entry an extremely broad security weakness. A single '+' character in /etc/hosts.equiv trusts every host on the network entirely. Penetration testers should always check for this file and its contents when R-services are found to be running.

questions.question: An attacker on the same network segment as a target running rlogin wants to exploit a trust relationship. The target's /etc/hosts.equiv contains the attacker's hostname. What is the most direct method of exploiting this?

options.A: Connect directly with rlogin specifying the trusted hostname to authenticate without a password
options.B: Perform a brute-force attack against the rlogin port using a wordlist of common passwords
options.C: Intercept the rlogin session with a man-in-the-middle proxy and inject commands at the TCP layer
options.D: Exploit the rlogin daemon's buffer overflow to bypass the hosts.equiv check entirely

questions.explanation: When a host appears in /etc/hosts.equiv, the rlogin and rsh daemons will accept connections from that host without prompting for a password, provided the username exists locally. An attacker who controls or can spoof a trusted hostname can simply run 'rlogin -l <username> <target>' and gain immediate shell access. This is a direct exploitation of the trust mechanism — no brute-force, proxy, or buffer overflow is required. This illustrates why R-services should be disabled entirely and replaced with SSH, which uses cryptographic authentication rather than name-based trust.

questions.question: The NIS (Network Information Service) system uses an RPC-based service called ypserv. What is the primary security risk of an exposed ypserv service on an untrusted network?

options.A: An unauthenticated attacker can query ypserv to retrieve the NIS password map, including hashed passwords
options.B: ypserv automatically grants root-level shell access to any host that connects on port 111
options.C: The ypserv service encrypts its responses with a static key that can be easily reversed
options.D: Querying ypserv causes the NIS master server to permanently delete its local password database

questions.explanation: NIS (sometimes called YP) distributes system configuration files — including /etc/passwd equivalents — across a network using RPC. The ypserv daemon does not implement authentication for map queries; any host that can reach the service and knows the NIS domain name can request maps. Using tools like 'ypcat passwd' or 'ypmatch', an attacker can retrieve the full NIS password map containing usernames and hashed passwords. These hashes can then be cracked offline. The NIS domain name is often trivially discoverable or guessable. This lack of authentication makes NIS fundamentally unsuitable for use on untrusted networks.

questions.question: During a network scan you discover that TCP and UDP port 111 is open on a target host. What is the significance of this port in the context of RPC enumeration?

options.A: Port 111 is the well-known port for rpcbind (portmapper), which registers and locates all other RPC services
options.B: Port 111 is reserved exclusively for the NFS daemon and indicates a directly mountable filesystem
options.C: Port 111 is used by the RPC encryption service to negotiate session keys for all downstream RPC calls
options.D: Port 111 is the default administrative port for the Sun RPC management console interface

questions.explanation: Port 111 (TCP and UDP) is the IANA-assigned port for the rpcbind service, also known as the portmapper. When an RPC service starts, it registers its program number and the dynamic port it is listening on with rpcbind. Clients query rpcbind on port 111 to discover the current port for a given RPC service. For a penetration tester, an open port 111 is a pivotal discovery: running 'rpcinfo -p <target>' will enumerate all registered RPC services (such as NFS, mountd, NIS/ypbind, rstatd, and others), their version numbers, and their current ports — providing a detailed map of the system's RPC attack surface.

questions.question: A corporate network uses a proxy server through which all employee web traffic must pass before reaching the internet. This proxy filters content and enforces acceptable use policies. What type of proxy is this?

options.A: A forward proxy, which acts on behalf of clients to access resources on external servers
options.B: A reverse proxy, which sits in front of internal servers and forwards inbound client requests
options.C: A transparent proxy, which intercepts outbound traffic at the network layer without requiring any client configuration
options.D: A SOCKS proxy, which operates exclusively at the transport layer using the SOCKS5 protocol

questions.explanation: A forward proxy is positioned between internal clients and the external internet. Clients are configured (or forced via network controls) to route their requests through it. The proxy makes requests on behalf of the client, allowing the organisation to filter, log, and control outbound traffic. This is distinct from a reverse proxy, which sits in front of servers to protect and load-balance them from inbound traffic. Understanding this distinction is important for testers because a misconfigured forward proxy can be abused for SSRF or to pivot to internal resources, while a misconfigured reverse proxy can expose backend server details.

questions.question: When a user types a URL into their browser and presses Enter, which sequence correctly describes the high-level HTTP request lifecycle before the page is rendered?

options.A: DNS resolution to get the server IP, TCP connection, TLS handshake (if HTTPS), HTTP request sent, server processes and returns HTTP response
options.B: ARP broadcast to find the web server, UDP datagram with the URL sent, server returns HTML in a single UDP packet
options.C: ICMP echo to verify the server is alive, direct IP connection without TCP, HTTP request embedded in an ICMP packet
options.D: The browser queries DHCP for the server address, opens an FTP session, and downloads the page as a binary file

questions.explanation: The HTTP request lifecycle follows a defined sequence: first, the client resolves the hostname to an IP address via DNS. A TCP three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) establishes the connection to the server on port 80 (HTTP) or 443 (HTTPS). For HTTPS, a TLS handshake then negotiates encryption parameters and authenticates the server's certificate. The browser then sends the HTTP request (e.g., GET / HTTP/1.1), and the server processes it and returns an HTTP response containing the status code, headers, and body. Understanding this lifecycle is essential for testers using intercepting proxies like Burp Suite, as each stage presents its own security considerations.

questions.question: An Apache web server has a .htaccess file in the web root that is intended to restrict access to an /admin directory. A misconfiguration prevents Apache from reading this file. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The Apache configuration sets 'AllowOverride None' for the directory, which prevents .htaccess files from being processed
options.B: The .htaccess file uses Windows-style CRLF line endings, which Apache on Linux cannot parse
options.C: Apache only processes .htaccess files in the server root directory, not in web application subdirectories
options.D: The .htaccess file must be digitally signed by the server's SSL certificate to be considered authoritative

questions.explanation: .htaccess files are Apache's per-directory configuration mechanism, allowing access controls, redirects, and rewrites to be defined at the directory level. However, their processing is governed by the 'AllowOverride' directive in the main Apache configuration (httpd.conf or a vhost block). If 'AllowOverride None' is set — which is actually the secure recommended default — Apache completely ignores .htaccess files in that directory tree. Administrators who rely on .htaccess for security controls but fail to set 'AllowOverride All' or the appropriate granular options will find those controls silently bypassed. Penetration testers should verify that .htaccess restrictions are actually being enforced and not overridden at the server level.

questions.question: A penetration tester sends a specially crafted request to an IIS web server and receives a response that reveals an 8.3 (short) filename for a file that is not directly browseable. Which vulnerability does this demonstrate?

options.A: The IIS Tilde Enumeration vulnerability, which allows discovery of files and directories using 8.3 short filename guessing
options.B: A directory traversal vulnerability that returns the server's NTFS MFT in the HTTP response body
options.C: HTTP response splitting caused by a CRLF injection in the short filename generation algorithm
options.D: An XML external entity injection triggered by submitting a tilde character in a SOAP request

questions.explanation: Windows NTFS generates short (8.3) filenames for backward compatibility. IIS on Windows exposes a vulnerability where sending a request containing a tilde character (~) followed by a partial filename (e.g., GET /secret~1/ HTTP/1.1) causes the server to respond differently depending on whether a matching 8.3 name exists. By iterating over characters and observing the difference between a 404 and a 400/403 response, an attacker can enumerate hidden files and directories — including those with restricted direct access. This is particularly useful for discovering backup files, configuration files, or sensitive resources that are not linked anywhere on the site. The fix is to disable 8.3 filename creation via the NtfsDisable8dot3NameCreation registry setting.

questions.question: An attacker injects XSLT transformation instructions into an XML document processed by a server-side XSLT engine. What is the most severe potential outcome of a successful XSLT injection?

options.A: Remote code execution on the server, as some XSLT processors support extension functions that can execute OS commands
options.B: Persistent cross-site scripting stored in the server's XML database for all subsequent visitors
options.C: Denial of service through an XML bomb that causes the XSLT processor to consume all available memory
options.D: Exfiltration of the server's TLS private key by reading it as a local file through the XSLT document() function

questions.explanation: XSLT (Extensible Stylesheet Language Transformations) is a language for transforming XML documents. When user-supplied data is incorporated into XSLT stylesheets without sanitisation, an attacker may be able to inject arbitrary XSLT instructions. The severity depends heavily on the XSLT processor and its configuration: some processors (such as Apache Xalan, Saxon, or libxslt with certain options) support extension functions or the xsl:include/xsl:import directives that can be abused to include external resources or, in the most severe cases, call native functions to execute operating system commands. Even without code execution, XSLT injection can enable SSRF and local file disclosure via the document() function. XSLT injection is distinct from XXE, though both involve XML processing vulnerabilities.

questions.question: An attacker injects the string 'Welcome, Admin!' into a web page, and the text is rendered as bold by the browser. No JavaScript executes. Which vulnerability class does this represent?

options.A: HTML injection, where attacker-controlled markup is rendered by the browser but no script is executed
options.B: Reflected cross-site scripting (XSS), where the injected payload executes in the victim's browser context
options.C: DOM-based XSS, where the payload is processed by client-side JavaScript without a server round-trip
options.D: CSS injection, where the attacker modifies the page's visual style by injecting stylesheet rules

questions.explanation: HTML injection and cross-site scripting (XSS) are related but distinct vulnerabilities. HTML injection occurs when an attacker can insert arbitrary HTML markup that the browser renders, but the injected content does not include (or cannot execute) JavaScript. The impact can still be significant: an attacker can deface content, create fake login forms to harvest credentials (phishing), or alter the page's visible structure. XSS requires the execution of script — typically JavaScript — within the victim's browser context, which allows cookie theft, session hijacking, and other dynamic attacks. The distinction matters for risk assessment and remediation: both require output encoding, but XSS carries a higher CVSS score due to its script-execution capability.

questions.question: A PHP application compares password hashes using the loose comparison operator (==). The stored hash for a user is '0e462097431906509019562988736854'. An attacker discovers they can authenticate by submitting any password whose MD5 hash also begins with '0e' followed by only digits. Which PHP behaviour explains this?

options.A: PHP type juggling interprets strings matching the pattern '0e[digits]' as scientific notation (zero to a power), so both sides evaluate to float 0 and the comparison returns true
options.B: PHP casts all hash strings to hexadecimal integers before comparison, and any hash beginning with '0e' overflows to zero
options.C: The loose equality operator == in PHP performs a substring match, so two strings sharing the same prefix are considered equal
options.D: PHP treats strings beginning with '0' as octal numbers, and all octal representations of MD5 hashes evaluate to the same value

questions.explanation: PHP's loose comparison operator (==) performs type coercion. When both operands are strings that look like numbers in scientific notation (e.g., '0e462097...' is interpreted as 0 × 10^462097), PHP converts them to floats. Since zero raised to any power is still zero, both sides become 0.0 and the comparison returns true. This is the classic 'magic hash' vulnerability: an attacker finds a password whose hash matches the '0e[digits]' pattern and bypasses authentication because 0 == 0. Real-world examples include MD5 and SHA-1 hashes that happen to start with '0e' followed entirely by digits. The fix is to always use the strict comparison operator (===), which compares both type and value without coercion, or better still, use hash_equals() for timing-safe comparison. This behaviour was changed in PHP 8.0 for integer-to-string comparisons, but '0e' string-to-string scientific notation coercion still applies to == in all PHP versions.

questions.question: An ASP.NET web application uses ViewState to persist page data across postbacks. A penetration tester wants to forge a malicious ViewState to exploit insecure deserialization. What must the tester obtain or bypass to forge a valid ViewState with a correct MAC signature?

options.A: The application's machineKey value, which is used to compute the ViewState MAC — if the key is leaked, hardcoded, or predictable, the attacker can forge valid signatures
options.B: The server's TLS private key, which ASP.NET uses to sign ViewState before transmitting it over HTTPS
options.C: The IIS application pool identity credentials, because ViewState MAC is derived from the Windows service account password hash
options.D: The .NET Framework version number, because ViewState MAC validation is only enabled in specific framework versions and disabled by default in all others

questions.explanation: ASP.NET ViewState is a Base64-encoded blob that stores page state between HTTP requests. ASP.NET appends a Message Authentication Code (MAC) computed using the machineKey from web.config (or auto-generated if not explicitly configured). ViewState MAC is enabled by default and mandatory in .NET 4.5.2 and later — it cannot be disabled. To forge a ViewState, an attacker must know the machineKey. This can happen when the key is hardcoded in web.config and exposed via information disclosure (e.g., directory traversal, misconfigured source control), when a default or example machineKey is used, or when the key is shared across a web farm and leaked from one node. With the machineKey, an attacker can craft a ViewState containing a malicious serialized object and compute a valid MAC, triggering insecure deserialization via ObjectStateFormatter — the basis of exploits like ysoserial.net's ViewState payloads.

questions.question: A Java application server exposes a JMX (Java Management Extensions) interface on the network without authentication. What is the most significant security risk this poses to a penetration tester?

options.A: An unauthenticated attacker can invoke MBean operations to deploy a malicious application or execute OS commands
options.B: JMX traffic is transmitted in cleartext UDP, allowing passive sniffing of all heap memory contents
options.C: The JMX agent automatically synchronises its configuration to all other JVMs on the same subnet
options.D: Connecting to the JMX port causes the JVM to generate a thread dump that overwrites the application logs

questions.explanation: JMX is a Java technology that provides tools for managing and monitoring Java applications, including the JVM itself. When the JMX remote interface is enabled without authentication (com.sun.management.jmxremote.authenticate=false) and without SSL, any network-reachable attacker can connect using a tool such as jconsole or mjet. Through JMX, an attacker can interact with MBeans (Managed Beans) exposed by the application server. On Tomcat, for example, the Catalina MBean provides a 'deploy' operation that can be used to deploy a malicious WAR file containing a web shell, resulting in remote code execution with the privileges of the JVM process. JMX exposure on application servers like JBoss/WildFly, WebLogic, and Tomcat has been the root cause of numerous high-profile compromises.

questions.question: In early versions of Ruby on Rails, a vulnerability allowed attackers to submit HTTP parameters that automatically set attributes on ActiveRecord model objects, bypassing developer-intended access controls. What is this vulnerability called?

options.A: Mass assignment, where user-supplied parameters are bound directly to model attributes without a whitelist
options.B: SQL injection via ActiveRecord, where ORM-generated queries are manipulated by malformed parameter names
options.C: Template injection in ERB views, where user parameters are evaluated as Ruby code during rendering
options.D: Insecure direct object reference, where an attacker modifies a numeric ID parameter to access another user's record

questions.explanation: Rails' ActiveRecord ORM includes a feature called mass assignment, which allows a controller to pass a hash of user-supplied parameters directly to a model's constructor or update method (e.g., User.new(params[:user])). If no attribute whitelist (attr_accessible) or blacklist (attr_protected) is configured, an attacker can include arbitrary attribute names in the request — including sensitive ones like 'admin', 'role', or 'is_active' — and have them set directly on the model object. The GitHub security incident of 2012 was a famous real-world example. Rails 4+ introduced Strong Parameters as a mandatory whitelist mechanism to address this. When testing Rails applications, testers should probe POST/PUT parameters by adding sensitive field names to see if they are accepted and persisted.

questions.question: A penetration tester obtains a Java applet from a web application. Which tool would be most appropriate for decompiling the applet's .class files back into readable source code?

options.A: Burp Suite's Decoder tool to base64-decode the bytecode
options.B: A Java decompiler such as CFR or Procyon to reconstruct Java source
options.C: Nmap's NSE scripting engine to extract embedded strings from memory
options.D: Wireshark to capture the applet's network traffic during execution

questions.explanation: Java .class files contain bytecode that can be decompiled back into near-original Java source code using tools like CFR, Procyon, or the older JAD. This is a significant security risk because client-side logic — including hard-coded credentials, API keys, validation routines, and business logic — becomes readable to an attacker. Java's bytecode is not obfuscated by default, making decompilation straightforward. Burp Suite handles HTTP traffic, Nmap is a network scanner, and Wireshark captures packets — none of these decompile bytecode.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the primary security risk associated with ActiveX controls in Internet Explorer?

options.A: ActiveX controls run in a sandboxed environment with no access to the OS
options.B: ActiveX controls are limited to reading cookies and cannot execute code
options.C: ActiveX controls can execute native code with the privileges of the browser user
options.D: ActiveX controls are blocked unless the site holds a valid TLS certificate

questions.explanation: ActiveX controls are Component Object Model (COM) objects that Internet Explorer can download and execute directly on the user's machine. Unlike sandboxed technologies such as JavaScript, ActiveX runs as native code with the full privileges of the logged-in user. This means a malicious or compromised ActiveX control can read files, install malware, or modify the registry. This is a key reason why ActiveX has been deprecated and removed from modern browsers. The security model relies entirely on the user accepting the control and the code-signing certificate being trusted, which is a weak boundary.

questions.question: During a session fixation attack, what action does the attacker take before the victim authenticates to the application?

options.A: The attacker brute-forces the victim's password using a list of common credentials
options.B: The attacker intercepts the victim's session cookie after login using XSS
options.C: The attacker pre-sets a known session token and tricks the victim into authenticating with it
options.D: The attacker replays a captured authentication request to hijack the established session

questions.explanation: In a session fixation attack, the attacker first obtains or sets a valid session token — for example by visiting the site themselves or by manipulating a URL parameter — and then tricks the victim into authenticating while using that known token (e.g., via a crafted link). Because the application does not regenerate the session ID upon login, the attacker already knows the session ID and can use it to access the authenticated session. The defence is to always issue a fresh session ID upon successful authentication. This is distinct from session hijacking (stealing a token post-login) or brute-forcing credentials.

questions.question: An application generates session tokens using a sequential counter combined with the current timestamp. Why is this considered a weak session management practice?

options.A: Sequential counters cause session tokens to exceed the maximum cookie size limit
options.B: Tokens based on predictable values can be guessed or calculated by an attacker
options.C: Timestamp-based tokens expire too quickly and cause usability problems for users
options.D: Combining two values creates tokens that are too long to be processed by web servers

questions.explanation: Session tokens must be unpredictable and contain sufficient entropy so they cannot be guessed or calculated. If a token is derived from a sequential counter or timestamp — both of which are observable or inferable — an attacker can enumerate token values to find valid sessions belonging to other users. A secure session token should be generated using a cryptographically secure pseudo-random number generator (CSPRNG) with at least 128 bits of entropy. Tools like Burp Suite's Sequencer can statistically analyse token randomness to identify predictable generation flaws.

questions.question: A web application returns a full Java stack trace to the user when an unhandled exception occurs. Which type of sensitive information is most likely exposed by this stack trace?

options.A: The plaintext password of the currently logged-in user session
options.B: The server's private TLS key used to decrypt HTTPS traffic
options.C: Internal class names, file paths, library versions, and server-side logic
options.D: The contents of all cookies associated with the current browser session

questions.explanation: Stack traces reveal detailed internal information about the application's structure, including fully-qualified class and method names, file system paths, framework and library versions, and the sequence of code execution that led to the error. This information is invaluable to an attacker during reconnaissance — library versions identify known CVEs, file paths reveal the server's directory structure, and class names expose framework choices. Stack traces should never be shown to end users; instead, applications should log errors server-side and display a generic, user-friendly error message with a reference ID.

questions.question: A web server is configured to display its default framework error pages rather than custom application error pages. What is the primary security concern with this configuration?

options.A: Default error pages consume significantly more server resources than custom pages
options.B: Default error pages may disclose server software, version numbers, and technology stack details
options.C: Default error pages prevent users from being redirected to the correct part of the site
options.D: Default error pages are rendered with higher privileges and can escalate a user's access

questions.explanation: Default error pages from web servers and frameworks (e.g., Apache's 404 page, IIS's 500 page, or a Django debug page) typically include the server software name, version number, and sometimes the underlying technology stack. This fingerprinting information allows an attacker to quickly identify the exact server version and search for known, unpatched CVEs against it. Custom error pages should be configured for all HTTP error codes (400, 403, 404, 500, etc.) to return a generic, non-descriptive message that gives no indication of the underlying technology.

questions.question: The POODLE attack against SSLv3 exploits which fundamental weakness in that protocol?

options.A: SSLv3 uses RSA key exchange exclusively, which is vulnerable to quantum decryption
options.B: SSLv3 CBC mode padding is not verified, allowing an attacker to decrypt cipher text byte by byte
options.C: SSLv3 certificates use MD5 signatures, enabling a hash collision to forge the server certificate
options.D: SSLv3 transmits the session master secret in cleartext during the initial handshake

questions.explanation: POODLE (Padding Oracle On Downgraded Legacy Encryption) exploits the fact that SSLv3's CBC mode does not properly define or verify padding bytes. An attacker who can perform a man-in-the-middle attack and trigger multiple requests (e.g., via JavaScript in the browser) can act as a padding oracle, decrypting one byte of ciphertext per 256 requests on average. The practical impact is that an attacker on the same network can decrypt sensitive values such as session cookies. The mitigation is to disable SSLv3 entirely on both servers and clients, and prefer TLS 1.2 or 1.3.

questions.question: A developer stores user-submitted data by applying Base64 encoding before saving it to the database. Why does this fail to provide confidentiality for that data?

options.A: Base64 increases data size by 33%, causing storage inefficiency but not a security risk
options.B: Base64 encoding is a reversible transformation with no secret key, not a cryptographic operation
options.C: Base64 is a symmetric encryption scheme, but its key is publicly known and easily reversed
options.D: Base64 only protects data in transit but not data at rest inside a database

questions.explanation: Base64 is an encoding scheme — it is a deterministic, keyless, fully reversible transformation designed for safe data transport in text-based protocols, not for confidentiality. Anyone who sees Base64-encoded data can decode it instantly using freely available tools. It provides no secrecy whatsoever. Encryption, by contrast, requires a secret key and a cryptographic algorithm (e.g., AES-256) to produce ciphertext that cannot be reversed without the key. Confusing encoding with encryption is a common developer mistake that leads to false confidence and data exposure.

questions.question: In a security-focused code review, what is 'taint analysis' primarily used to identify?

options.A: Memory regions that have been freed twice, leading to heap corruption vulnerabilities
options.B: Third-party library dependencies that have known CVEs published against them
options.C: Untrusted user-controlled input that flows into sensitive operations without sanitisation
options.D: Functions that execute with elevated privileges without proper authorisation checks

questions.explanation: Taint analysis is a code review technique — used in both manual review and Static Application Security Testing (SAST) tools — that tracks untrusted data (the 'taint source', typically user input from HTTP parameters, headers, or cookies) as it flows through the application to sensitive 'sink' functions (e.g., SQL query execution, OS command execution, HTML rendering, file path construction). If tainted data reaches a sink without passing through a sanitisation or validation step (a 'sanitiser'), it indicates a potential injection vulnerability such as SQLi, XSS, or command injection. Taint analysis is one of the most powerful techniques for finding injection flaws programmatically.

questions.question: What is the primary operational difference between Static Application Security Testing (SAST) and Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST)?

options.A: SAST requires a running application; DAST analyses compiled binaries without execution
options.B: SAST analyses source code or binaries without execution; DAST tests the running application from the outside
options.C: SAST is performed by developers; DAST must legally only be performed by certified testers
options.D: SAST identifies network-level vulnerabilities; DAST identifies code-level logic flaws

questions.explanation: SAST (Static Analysis) examines source code, bytecode, or compiled binaries without executing the application — it can be integrated into a CI/CD pipeline and run early in the SDLC before deployment. It is effective at finding code-level flaws like injection points, hard-coded secrets, and insecure function usage. DAST (Dynamic Analysis) tests a live, running application from the outside, simulating an attacker without access to source code. It finds runtime vulnerabilities such as authentication issues, misconfigurations, and injection flaws that are observable via application responses. Both approaches are complementary; SAST has false positives while DAST may miss issues only visible in source code.

questions.question: When using Burp Suite's crawler (spider) during a web application assessment, what is the primary security-relevant output it provides?

options.A: A list of open TCP ports and services running on the web server's host
options.B: A map of discovered application content including URLs, parameters, and forms
options.C: Automated exploitation of all SQL injection points found on the target site
options.D: A certificate transparency log showing all subdomains registered for the domain

questions.explanation: Burp Suite's crawler systematically browses a web application, following links, submitting forms, and parsing JavaScript to build a comprehensive site map of all discoverable content — including URLs, query parameters, POST parameters, and entry points. This is essential in the reconnaissance phase of a web assessment to understand the attack surface before manually probing individual functions. It does not perform port scanning (that is Nmap's role), does not automatically exploit injections (that is active scanning or manual testing), and does not enumerate DNS subdomains.

questions.question: During forced browsing of a web application, which of the following file extensions is most worth checking for, as it may expose application source code or database credentials?

options.A: Extensions such as .bak, .old, .orig, or .swp left by editors or backup processes
options.B: Extensions such as .png, .jpg, or .gif used for static image assets
options.C: Extensions such as .html or .htm used for static informational pages
options.D: Extensions such as .css or .js used for client-side styling and behaviour

questions.explanation: Backup and temporary file extensions (.bak, .old, .orig, .copy, .swp, .~) are frequently left on web servers accidentally by developers or deployment processes. When a file such as config.php.bak or database.old is accessible via the web root, it may serve the raw source code — including hard-coded database credentials, API keys, or application logic — rather than executing server-side. These files are a high-value target during forced browsing. Tools like dirb, gobuster, and Burp Suite's content discovery can use wordlists that include these extensions. Static assets like images, CSS, and JS are expected to be public and carry less sensitive risk.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes how a DOM-based XSS vulnerability differs from reflected or stored XSS?

options.A: DOM-based XSS requires the attacker to have write access to the web server's file system
options.B: DOM-based XSS payload executes via client-side JavaScript reading from an attacker-controlled source such as the URL fragment
options.C: DOM-based XSS is only exploitable when the target browser has JavaScript disabled
options.D: DOM-based XSS payloads are stored server-side and served to every subsequent visitor

questions.explanation: DOM-based XSS occurs entirely on the client side. Vulnerable JavaScript code reads data from an attacker-controllable 'source' — such as document.location, document.URL, location.hash, or document.referrer — and passes it unsanitised to a dangerous 'sink' such as innerHTML, document.write(), or eval(). Because the payload may never be sent to the server (e.g., using the URL fragment #), it can bypass server-side input validation and Web Application Firewalls. Reflected XSS is echoed by the server in its response; stored XSS is persisted in a database. DOM XSS is a client-side code injection flaw requiring careful review of JavaScript source.

questions.question: A security engineer wants to reduce the risk of XSS attacks against a web application. Which HTTP response header, when correctly configured, provides the most direct mitigation by controlling which script sources the browser will trust?

options.A: Strict-Transport-Security, which forces the browser to use HTTPS for all future requests
options.B: X-Frame-Options, which prevents the page from being embedded in an iframe on another origin
options.C: Content-Security-Policy, which defines an allowlist of trusted sources for scripts and other resources
options.D: X-Content-Type-Options, which prevents the browser from MIME-sniffing the response content type

questions.explanation: Content-Security-Policy (CSP) is the primary browser-enforced defence against XSS. A correctly configured CSP header uses directives such as script-src to define an explicit allowlist of origins from which scripts may be loaded or executed. Inline scripts and eval() can be blocked by omitting 'unsafe-inline' and 'unsafe-eval'. When an injected script attempts to execute or load from an untrusted source, the browser blocks it and reports the violation. While CSP is a powerful defence-in-depth control, it does not replace input validation and output encoding. HSTS protects against protocol downgrade attacks, X-Frame-Options prevents clickjacking, and X-Content-Type-Options prevents MIME confusion attacks.

questions.question: During a SQL injection assessment, a tester appends the payload ' UNION SELECT username, password FROM users-- to a parameter. What is the attacker attempting to achieve?

options.A: Terminate the current database connection and force the server to reconnect
options.B: Append results from a second SELECT query to the original query's output to extract table data
options.C: Insert a new row into the users table containing a known username and password
options.D: Drop the users table by chaining a destructive statement after the original query

questions.explanation: UNION-based SQL injection exploits the SQL UNION operator, which combines the result sets of two SELECT statements into a single response. The attacker appends a second SELECT that targets sensitive tables (such as users, credentials, or accounts) and the application then returns both result sets in its response — often visible in the web page output. Prerequisites are that the injected UNION SELECT must have the same number of columns as the original query and compatible data types. The comment sequence (-- or #) terminates the rest of the original query to prevent syntax errors. This technique requires the application to reflect query results back to the user.

questions.question: A tester suspects blind SQL injection exists in a login form but the application returns an identical response for both valid and invalid input. Which technique can be used to confirm the vulnerability without visible output?

options.A: Submitting an HTTP OPTIONS request to check which methods the server supports
options.B: Injecting a time-delay payload such as '; WAITFOR DELAY '0:0:5'-- and measuring the server response time
options.C: Encoding the SQL payload in Base64 to bypass the application's input validation filter
options.D: Using a UNION SELECT statement to redirect database output into an HTTP response header

questions.explanation: Time-based blind SQL injection infers the existence of a vulnerability through deliberate server-side delays rather than visible output differences. Payloads like WAITFOR DELAY '0:0:5'-- (MS SQL Server), SLEEP(5)-- (MySQL), or pg_sleep(5)-- (PostgreSQL) instruct the database to pause before responding. If the response takes approximately 5 seconds longer than normal, the payload was executed by the database engine, confirming injection. This technique is essential when the application does not reflect errors or data but is still passing unsanitised input to SQL. Tools like sqlmap automate this detection process.

questions.question: What distinguishes second-order SQL injection from first-order (standard) SQL injection?

options.A: Second-order SQLi requires two separate database servers to be present in the infrastructure
options.B: Second-order SQLi involves malicious input that is stored safely, then executed unsafely when retrieved in a later operation
options.C: Second-order SQLi exclusively targets stored procedures and cannot affect dynamic SQL queries
options.D: Second-order SQLi bypasses parameterised queries by injecting into database stored in environment variables

questions.explanation: Second-order SQL injection (also called stored SQL injection) occurs in two stages. First, an attacker submits malicious input that the application stores in the database — it may appear safe at this point because it is inserted using a parameterised query or properly escaped. Second, a different part of the application later retrieves that stored value and incorporates it into a new SQL query, this time without proper escaping, causing injection. This is particularly insidious because security testing that only examines the input stage will miss the vulnerability. A classic example is a username like admin'-- that is safely inserted but later used unsanitised in a profile update query.

questions.question: How does Burp Suite's intercepting proxy assist a penetration tester when assessing a web application for parameter manipulation vulnerabilities?

options.A: It automatically injects all known SQL injection payloads into every parameter it observes
options.B: It sits between the browser and server, allowing the tester to view and modify HTTP requests before they are sent
options.C: It replaces the browser's TLS stack to issue self-signed certificates for all visited domains
options.D: It scans the server's file system for writable directories that could be exploited via file upload

questions.explanation: Burp Suite's Proxy module positions itself as a man-in-the-middle between the tester's browser and the target server. All HTTP/S requests and responses pass through it, and the tester can pause ('intercept') any request to inspect and manually modify parameters — including GET/POST parameters, HTTP headers, cookies, and JSON/XML body content — before forwarding to the server. This is fundamental for parameter manipulation testing: changing a price from 100 to 1, modifying a role field from user to admin, or altering a hidden form field. The proxy does not automatically inject payloads (that is Burp Scanner/Intruder), does not issue certificates in a malicious sense, and does not interact with the server's file system.

questions.question: A web application stores the user's account type in a cookie as accountType=standard. What vulnerability is a penetration tester investigating if they modify this cookie value to accountType=admin?

options.A: Cross-Site Request Forgery, where a forged request is submitted from another domain
options.B: Insecure Direct Object Reference, where a user-controlled identifier is changed to access another user's resources
options.C: Insecure client-side trust, where the server accepts tampered cookie parameters as authoritative
options.D: Session fixation, where a known session ID is set before the victim authenticates

questions.explanation: Storing access-control decisions such as account type, role, or privilege level in client-side cookies and trusting those values server-side without server-side validation is a fundamental insecure design flaw. Cookies are fully controllable by the client — they can be read, modified, and replayed using browser developer tools or an intercepting proxy like Burp Suite. If the server promotes the user's privileges based solely on the tampered cookie value, an attacker can escalate privileges without any server-side authorisation bypass. All authorisation decisions must be made server-side based on the authenticated session identity, not on client-supplied parameter values.

questions.question: During an Oracle database assessment, a tester attempts to enumerate valid SIDs (System Identifiers) on the target host. Which tool or technique is commonly used for this purpose against the TNS Listener?

options.A: Sending HTTP TRACE requests to the database port to reflect SID values in the response
options.B: Using Metasploit's oracle_sid_brute module or tnscmd.pl to query the listener for registered services
options.C: Performing a DNS zone transfer against the database server's hostname to list SID records
options.D: Submitting an LDAP query to the database port to enumerate all registered SID entries

questions.explanation: The Oracle TNS Listener maintains a list of registered database services (SIDs and service names). On older or misconfigured Oracle installations, the listener will respond to unauthenticated STATUS commands that reveal registered SIDs. Tools such as tnscmd.pl, Metasploit's auxiliary/scanner/oracle/oracle_sid module (oracle_sid_brute), and oscanner can query or brute-force SID names. Knowing the SID is a prerequisite for connecting to the Oracle database. In newer Oracle versions (10g+), the listener password protects this, but many deployments remain misconfigured. DNS zone transfers, HTTP TRACE, and LDAP are unrelated to Oracle SID enumeration.

questions.question: An attacker has gained access to an Oracle database account with execute privileges on DBMS_SCHEDULER. How could this potentially be escalated?

options.A: DBMS_SCHEDULER allows the user to export the entire database to an external FTP server
options.B: DBMS_SCHEDULER can be used to create jobs that execute operating system commands with Oracle process privileges
options.C: DBMS_SCHEDULER enables the user to reset any other database user's password without DBA rights
options.D: DBMS_SCHEDULER permits direct reads from the Oracle password hash file on the server filesystem

questions.explanation: Oracle's DBMS_SCHEDULER package allows privileged database users to create and run scheduled jobs. Critically, it supports job types that execute external programs or OS scripts (EXECUTABLE type jobs). If the Oracle database process runs with elevated OS privileges (which is common in default installations), an attacker with EXECUTE on DBMS_SCHEDULER can schedule a job to run an OS command — such as adding a user, spawning a reverse shell, or reading sensitive files — with the Oracle process's operating system privileges. This represents a path from database user to OS-level access. The privilege is often granted to application service accounts that should not require it, making it a key escalation vector.

questions.question: Microsoft SQL Server can be configured to use 'Mixed Mode Authentication'. What security concern does this introduce compared to 'Windows Authentication Only' mode?

options.A: Mixed Mode disables TLS encryption for all database connections regardless of client configuration
options.B: Mixed Mode enables the SQL Server 'sa' account and SQL-native logins, which use weaker credential storage than Windows authentication
options.C: Mixed Mode forces all connections to use a shared service account, eliminating individual user accountability
options.D: Mixed Mode allows database connections from any IP address without requiring a network firewall rule

questions.explanation: SQL Server Mixed Mode Authentication enables both Windows Authentication (Kerberos/NTLM-integrated) and SQL Server native logins (username and password stored within SQL Server itself). This introduces the 'sa' (system administrator) account, which has full sysadmin rights and a fixed name — making it a prime brute-force target. SQL logins also historically used weaker password hashing (PWDENCRYPT) and are not subject to domain password policies by default. Windows Authentication is generally preferred because it leverages Active Directory's centralised policy, Kerberos, and does not transmit passwords directly. If Mixed Mode is required, the 'sa' account should be disabled and strong passwords enforced on all SQL logins.

questions.question: A penetration tester discovers that an application's ODBC connection string is stored in a plaintext configuration file on the web server. What is the primary risk of this finding?

options.A: The ODBC driver version in the connection string may be incompatible with the current database server
options.B: The connection string exposes the database hostname, port, database name, username, and password to anyone who can read the file
options.C: Storing ODBC connection strings in files causes the database to reject connections from the application
options.D: The plaintext file will cause the web server to cache the database credentials in browser history

questions.explanation: An ODBC (Open Database Connectivity) connection string typically contains all information needed to connect to a database: the driver type, server hostname or IP, port, database name, and authentication credentials (username and password). When stored in a plaintext configuration file (such as web.config, app.config, or a .ini file), any user or process that can read the file — including via a Local File Inclusion vulnerability, a misconfigured web server, or direct server access — can extract full database credentials. These credentials can then be used to connect to the database directly and access or exfiltrate all data. Connection strings should be encrypted at rest using platform-specific secret management (e.g., Windows DPAPI, environment variables, or a secrets vault).

questions.question: Which of the following are common security vulnerabilities associated with the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP)?

options.A: DHCP Starvation and Rogue DHCP Server attacks
options.B: IP Address Spoofing and MAC Address Flooding
options.C: DNS Cache Poisoning and ARP Cache Poisoning
options.D: TCP Sequence Number Prediction and Session Hijacking

questions.explanation: DHCP is vulnerable to several attacks because it lacks built-in authentication. DHCP Starvation involves an attacker exhausting the pool of available IP addresses by sending numerous DHCP requests with spoofed MAC addresses, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS) for legitimate clients. A Rogue DHCP Server attack occurs when an unauthorized server responds to DHCP requests, potentially providing clients with incorrect gateway or DNS information to facilitate Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks. While IP spoofing and ARP poisoning are related network attacks, they are not primary DHCP-specific vulnerabilities.

questions.question: What is the primary objective of a DHCP Starvation attack?

options.A: To intercept and modify DHCP traffic between clients and the server
options.B: To exhaust the pool of available IP addresses on a DHCP server
options.C: To redirect client traffic to a malicious gateway by spoofing DHCP responses
options.D: To crash the DHCP server by sending malformed packets to UDP port 67

questions.explanation: In a DHCP Starvation attack, the attacker floods the DHCP server with DHCPDISCOVER messages, each using a unique, spoofed MAC address. The goal is to consume all available IP addresses in the server's scope. Once the pool is exhausted, legitimate clients are unable to obtain or renew IP addresses, resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS) for new network connections. This attack is often a precursor to a Rogue DHCP Server attack, as it clears the way for the attacker's server to respond to new requests.

questions.question: How does a Rogue DHCP Server attack typically facilitate a Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) scenario?

options.A: By exhausting the legitimate DHCP server's IP pool using spoofed MAC addresses
options.B: By providing clients with the attacker's IP address as the default gateway or DNS server
options.C: By sniffing DHCP traffic to capture sensitive information like usernames and passwords
options.D: By injecting malicious code into the DHCP lease acknowledgment packets sent to clients

questions.explanation: A Rogue DHCP Server is an unauthorized DHCP server introduced into a network. When a client broadcasts a DHCP request, the rogue server attempts to respond faster than the legitimate server. If successful, it can provide the client with a lease that includes malicious configuration settings, such as the attacker's IP address as the default gateway or a malicious DNS server. This allows the attacker to intercept, inspect, or modify the client's outbound traffic, effectively establishing a Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) position.

questions.question: What is the primary function of the Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP)?

options.A: To dynamically assign IP addresses to Cisco devices on a local network
options.B: To share information about directly connected Cisco equipment with other Cisco devices
options.C: To provide secure remote management access to Cisco routers and switches
options.D: To route traffic between different VLANs within a Cisco-based enterprise network

questions.explanation: Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP) is a proprietary Layer 2 protocol used by Cisco devices to share information with directly connected neighbors. It operates independently of Layer 3 protocols and provides details such as the device ID, software version, hardware platform, and capabilities of the neighboring device. While useful for network management and troubleshooting, CDP can also be exploited by attackers to gather reconnaissance data about the network infrastructure.

questions.question: What does the acronym CDP stand for in the context of Cisco networking?

options.A: Cisco Device Protocol
options.B: Cisco Discovery Protocol
options.C: Centralized Discovery Protocol
options.D: Cisco Deployment Protocol

questions.explanation: CDP stands for Cisco Discovery Protocol. It is a proprietary data link layer protocol developed by Cisco Systems to facilitate the discovery of Cisco devices on a network. It is enabled by default on most Cisco equipment and provides valuable information for network administrators to map out their network topology.

questions.question: Which of the following are potential security risks associated with leaving CDP enabled on a network interface?

options.A: Information disclosure and CDP spoofing attacks
options.B: MAC address table exhaustion and VLAN hopping
options.C: Brute-force attacks against the device's management console
options.D: Denial of Service attacks targeting the device's routing table

questions.explanation: CDP transmits sensitive information in plaintext, including device models, IOS versions, and IP addresses of management interfaces. This leads to information disclosure, which attackers can use for reconnaissance. Additionally, an attacker can perform CDP spoofing by sending forged CDP packets to trick other devices into believing a legitimate Cisco device is connected, potentially facilitating further attacks or misconfigurations. It is a best practice to disable CDP on untrusted or user-facing interfaces.

questions.question: What is the primary goal of a CDP Spoofing attack?

options.A: To crash a Cisco device by flooding it with malformed CDP packets
options.B: To forge CDP packets to misinform neighboring Cisco devices about a connection
options.C: To capture and decrypt CDP traffic to obtain management credentials
options.D: To bypass port security by mimicking the MAC address of a Cisco device

questions.explanation: In a CDP Spoofing attack, an attacker sends forged CDP packets into the network. These packets contain fabricated information about a non-existent or malicious Cisco device. Neighboring Cisco devices that receive these packets will add the spoofed device to their CDP neighbor table. This can be used to misinform network administrators, disrupt network mapping tools, or potentially influence other protocols that rely on CDP information for configuration.

questions.question: How can an attacker exploit CDP for information disclosure during the reconnaissance phase?

options.A: By intercepting CDP packets to identify device models and software versions
options.B: By using CDP to remotely execute commands on a Cisco switch or router
options.C: By injecting malicious configuration commands into legitimate CDP advertisements
options.D: By exploiting a buffer overflow vulnerability in the CDP processing engine

questions.explanation: CDP advertisements are sent as multicast frames in plaintext. An attacker connected to the same network segment can easily capture these frames using a packet sniffer. The information contained within CDP packets—such as the device ID, hardware platform, software version, and IP addresses—provides a wealth of reconnaissance data. This allows an attacker to identify specific vulnerabilities associated with the discovered hardware and software versions, making their subsequent attacks more targeted and effective.

questions.question: What does the acronym HSRP stand for in Cisco networking?

options.A: High Speed Routing Protocol
options.B: Hot Standby Router Protocol
options.C: High Security Routing Protocol
options.D: Host Standby Redundancy Protocol

questions.explanation: HSRP stands for Hot Standby Router Protocol. It is a Cisco proprietary redundancy protocol that allows multiple routers to work together to present the appearance of a single virtual default gateway to hosts on a LAN. This ensures high availability by providing a failover mechanism if the primary (active) router fails.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the Hot Standby Router Protocol (HSRP)?

options.A: To provide load balancing across multiple active routers on a network
options.B: To provide default gateway redundancy for IP hosts on a local area network
options.C: To encrypt routing updates between Cisco routers to prevent eavesdropping
options.D: To dynamically assign IP addresses to clients in a high-availability environment

questions.explanation: HSRP is designed to provide high availability for the default gateway. It groups multiple physical routers into a single virtual router with a shared virtual IP and MAC address. One router is elected as 'Active' and handles all traffic sent to the virtual gateway, while another is 'Standby', ready to take over immediately if the active router fails. This process is transparent to the end hosts, ensuring continuous network connectivity.

questions.question: Which UDP port is used by the Hot Standby Router Protocol (HSRP) for sending hello messages?

options.A: UDP port 1985
options.B: UDP port 1986
options.C: UDP port 2022
options.D: UDP port 1701

questions.explanation: HSRP uses UDP port 1985 for its communication. Routers in an HSRP group send 'hello' packets to the multicast address 224.0.0.2 (HSRPv1) or 224.0.0.102 (HSRPv2) on this port to communicate their priority and state (Active, Standby, or Speak). Monitoring this port can allow an attacker to discover HSRP configurations on the network.

questions.question: What are the primary security vulnerabilities associated with the default configuration of HSRP?

options.A: Lack of authentication and susceptibility to HSRP spoofing
options.B: Weak encryption of routing updates and session hijacking
options.C: Vulnerability to buffer overflows in the hello packet parser
options.D: Susceptibility to MAC address flooding on the virtual interface

questions.explanation: By default, HSRP often uses either no authentication or a simple plaintext password ('cisco' is a common default). This lack of strong authentication allows an attacker to perform HSRP spoofing. An attacker can send forged HSRP hello packets with a higher priority than the current active router, tricking the group into electing the attacker's machine as the new active router. This facilitates a Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attack as all traffic destined for the virtual gateway will be routed through the attacker.

questions.question: In the context of HSRP, what does 'Lack of Authentication' typically refer to?

options.A: The protocol does not support any form of password protection for hello messages
options.B: The use of plaintext passwords or no password at all for HSRP group communication
options.C: The inability of HSRP to integrate with external AAA servers like RADIUS or TACACS+
options.D: The failure of the protocol to verify the identity of the virtual gateway's MAC address

questions.explanation: Lack of authentication in HSRP usually means that the protocol is either configured with no authentication or uses 'Plaintext Authentication'. In the latter case, the authentication string is sent in the clear within every HSRP packet. An attacker can easily sniff this string and then use it to send valid-looking but malicious HSRP packets to the group, potentially taking over the Active router role.

questions.question: How does an attacker execute an HSRP Spoofing attack?

options.A: By flooding the network with HSRP hello packets to cause a Denial of Service
options.B: By sending forged HSRP hello packets with a higher priority to become the Active router
options.C: By intercepting and modifying HSRP packets to change the virtual IP address
options.D: By exploiting a vulnerability in the HSRP state machine to force a constant re-election

questions.explanation: An HSRP Spoofing attack involves the attacker sending forged HSRP hello messages to the multicast address used by the HSRP group. The attacker sets the priority in these forged packets to a value higher than that of the current Active router (default priority is 100). If HSRP preemption is enabled, the group will elect the attacker's machine as the new Active router. The attacker then becomes the default gateway for the segment, allowing them to intercept or manipulate all outbound traffic.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP)?

options.A: To provide load balancing for web traffic across multiple server instances
options.B: To provide high availability for default gateways using an open standard protocol
options.C: To encrypt all traffic passing through a virtual router to ensure data confidentiality
options.D: To dynamically assign VLAN memberships to ports based on the connected device

questions.explanation: VRRP is an open standard protocol (defined in RFC 5798) that provides for the automatic assignment of available IP routers to participating hosts. It is very similar in function to Cisco's HSRP, allowing multiple routers to form a single virtual router to provide redundancy for the default gateway. If the master router fails, a backup router automatically takes over the virtual IP address.

questions.question: What does the acronym VRRP stand for in network redundancy?

options.A: Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol
options.B: Virtual Routing and Redundancy Protocol
options.C: Variable Router Redundancy Protocol
options.D: Virtual Remote Redundancy Protocol

questions.explanation: VRRP stands for Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol. It is an industry-standard protocol used to increase the availability of the default gateway servicing hosts on the same subnet.

questions.question: Which of the following are common security concerns when implementing VRRP?

options.A: Weak or no authentication and susceptibility to VRRP spoofing
options.B: Lack of support for IPv6 and vulnerability to fragmentation attacks
options.C: Incompatibility with standard firewall rules and session timeout issues
options.D: High overhead on the router's CPU due to frequent advertisement packets

questions.explanation: Like HSRP, VRRP is susceptible to spoofing if not properly secured. If authentication is disabled or uses a weak method (like plaintext), an attacker can send forged VRRP advertisements with a higher priority to become the 'Master' router. This allows the attacker to intercept all traffic sent to the virtual IP address. Modern implementations recommend using IPsec or strong authentication if supported, though many deployments still rely on simple or no authentication.

questions.question: How can an attacker perform a VRRP Spoofing attack?

options.A: By flooding the network with VRRP advertisements to trigger a DoS condition
options.B: By sending forged VRRP advertisements with a higher priority to become the Master router
options.C: By capturing VRRP packets and replaying them to disrupt the election process
options.D: By modifying the VRRP configuration on a compromised router to point to a rogue IP

questions.explanation: In a VRRP Spoofing attack, the attacker sends forged VRRP advertisement packets. By setting the priority in these packets to 255 (the highest possible value) or simply a value higher than the current Master, the attacker can force an election and become the Master router for the virtual group. This positions the attacker as the default gateway for the network segment, enabling Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks.

questions.question: What security risk is introduced by using 'Simple Password' authentication in VRRP?

options.A: The password can be easily guessed using a dictionary attack against the router
options.B: The password is sent in plaintext and can be captured by anyone sniffing the network
options.C: The password only protects the control plane and does not secure the data plane
options.D: The use of a simple password disables all other security features within the protocol

questions.explanation: VRRP's 'Simple Password' authentication method sends the password in plaintext within the VRRP advertisement packets. Any attacker with access to the local network segment can use a packet sniffer to capture these packets and read the password. Once the password is known, the attacker can send valid, authenticated VRRP packets to perform spoofing or other disruptive actions. This method provides very little actual security against a determined attacker.

questions.question: What does the acronym VTP stand for in Cisco switching?

options.A: Virtual Trunking Protocol
options.B: VLAN Trunking Protocol
options.C: Variable Trunking Protocol
options.D: Virtual Terminal Protocol

questions.explanation: VTP stands for VLAN Trunking Protocol. It is a Cisco proprietary protocol used to synchronize VLAN information (such as VLAN IDs and names) across a group of Cisco switches within the same VTP domain. This simplifies VLAN management by allowing an administrator to create or delete a VLAN on one switch and have that change propagate to all other switches in the domain.

questions.question: What is the primary mechanism behind a VTP Manipulation attack?

options.A: An attacker floods the network with VTP advertisements to cause a switch to crash
options.B: An attacker introduces a rogue switch with a higher VTP revision number to overwrite VLAN configurations
options.C: An attacker intercepts VTP packets and modifies the VLAN names to cause network confusion
options.D: An attacker uses VTP to bypass port security and gain unauthorized access to a restricted VLAN

questions.explanation: In a VTP Manipulation attack, an attacker connects a rogue switch to the network and configures it with a higher VTP revision number than the current switches in the domain. When the rogue switch sends a VTP advertisement, all other switches in the domain will adopt its VLAN configuration, potentially deleting existing VLANs or modifying their settings. This can lead to widespread network disruption and Denial of Service (DoS).

questions.question: What does the acronym STP stand for in Ethernet networking?

options.A: Secure Transport Protocol
options.B: Spanning Tree Protocol
options.C: Standard Trunking Protocol
options.D: Switching Topology Protocol

questions.explanation: STP stands for Spanning Tree Protocol. It is a Layer 2 network protocol (IEEE 802.1D) that ensures a loop-free topology for Ethernet networks by managing redundant links and placing certain ports in a blocking state.

questions.question: What is the primary function of the Spanning Tree Protocol (STP)?

options.A: To provide high-speed data transmission between switches using link aggregation
options.B: To prevent network loops in Ethernet topologies by managing redundant links
options.C: To dynamically assign IP addresses to devices based on their physical location
options.D: To encrypt traffic between switches to prevent eavesdropping on the local network

questions.explanation: STP's primary role is to prevent broadcast storms and network instability caused by Layer 2 loops. It does this by identifying redundant paths in a network and logically disabling (blocking) specific ports to create a single, loop-free path between all switches. If a link fails, STP automatically recalculates the topology and enables a previously blocked port to restore connectivity.

questions.question: Which of the following are common security vulnerabilities associated with STP?
